Lessons.Title: Equations and Their Solutions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: decide whether a number solves a one-variable equation and whether an ordered pair solves a two-variable equation, and explain a solution's meaning in context. Edulytiks first-party source-aligned instruction, Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 4, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/4/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Official Addressing HSA-REI.A, HSA-REI.B.3. The source emphasizes checking and reasoning rather than just a mechanical solve procedure.

Original scenario: a bicycle technician charges a $12 service visit and $18 per hour. Total bill T=12+18h dollars for h≥0 hours. For bill T=66, substitute h=3 to verify 12+54=66; h=2 does not satisfy because total would be $48. A pair (3,66) solves T=12+18h, but (2,66) is not on the graph.

Student task: evaluate the truth of candidate solutions in one-variable and two-variable equations, explain why an incorrect candidate fails, then write a different plausible billing context. Compare numeric checks with reasoning about units; a graph point always uses coordinates in the correct order.

Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): interprets one-variable solution, verifies one true and one false candidate with substitution, interprets an ordered pair and domain, and gives a coherent contextual explanation. A multiple-choice check alone does not replace the source reasoning.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solution of equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A solution is a value (or ordered pair) making both sides equal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two-variable solution
KeyConcepts.Definition: An ordered pair makes an equation in two variables true.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Match variables to coordinates and units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Context limits meaningful values even when algebra accepts more.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State h≥0 when h is hours worked.
KeyConcepts.Example: h=-2 may solve a manipulated equation but cannot be a realistic positive work duration.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test two candidate values
WorkedExamples.Question: Does h=3 or h=2 solve 12+18h=66?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: Since only one candidate produces equality, h=3 is a solution and h=2 is not.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find the service hours
WorkedExamples.Question: A $66 bill follows T=12+18h. Find h.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Verify a graph point
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (4,84) on the graph T=12+18h?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: Interpret ordered pair h=4 hours, T=$84.
Compare this with claimed T=84; equal.
Thus the point is part of the relation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both values have the proper units and satisfy the equation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Only substituting into an equation after incorrect rearrangement
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Algebraic mistakes could give a spurious result.
A point (T,h) cannot be read as (h,T).
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label both axes and variable order.

SummaryPoints: A one-variable solution is a valid input making an equation true.
A two-variable solution is an ordered pair that satisfies the relation.
Check candidates directly and interpret their context and units.
